vignette:
He was twenty-seven when it happened, a quiet Tuesday afternoon in late October. The train was moving at standard speed through the industrial stretch east of the city, a section of track he knew by heart from five years on the line. He remembers the exact second he saw the figure step off the platform. There was no hesitation, no stumble. The man simply walked into the path of the locomotive, his coat flaring behind him like a dark wing. The emergency brake locked in his hand before he could think, but the train needed four hundred meters to stop. He felt the impact through the soles of his boots-a heavy, muffled thud that traveled up through the frame and into his chest.

He stayed on the job that day. He gave his statement to the transit police. He filled out the paperwork. He went home and took a shower, and that night he lay awake with the thud still in him, replaying the moment over and over, trying to see if there was something he could have done earlier-a horn, a shout, anything. But there was no warning. The man on the platform had been still, just standing with his hands in his pockets, looking out at the tracks. Nothing unusual, until he wasn't.

Now, two years later, he still works the same route. He thinks about quitting often, but he cannot picture another life. The job pays well, and it was his father's before him. But the train has become a different place. Every station approach makes his stomach clench. He finds himself scanning the platforms obsessively, cataloguing every passenger who stands too close to the yellow line, every person who looks down at the rails with a blank expression. He has developed a habit of tapping the brake lever with his fingers, gently, as if testing its readiness, even when there is no reason.

His sleep is broken. He wakes most nights with the thud in his chest, drenched in sweat, heart hammering. Sometimes the dream is not exactly the event-it is a version where the man turns at the last second, or where he himself is the one standing on the edge, watching the train come. He avoids the break room at the depot because of a particular photograph on the wall, a black-and-white of the old station in the 1970s, and he cannot explain why. He no longer eats lunch in his car because the silence makes the thud too loud. So he eats standing up, in the crowded crew room, not tasting anything.

His relationships have thinned. His friends stopped calling after he cancelled too many plans. He tells himself he likes the quiet, but the quiet is where the flashbacks live. His mother worries. She left messages asking if he is eating, if he wants her to make maqluba. He lets them pile up. When he does answer, he speaks in short, flat sentences. The effort of sounding fine exhausts him.

On the train, he has learned to keep his face calm. Passengers see a uniform, a conductor checking tickets, the usual. They do not see the way his eyes sweep the aisles for anything unusual, the way he braces every time the train slows near a crossing. He has started arriving an hour early for every shift so he can walk the length of the platform first, checking for anything that feels wrong. The other conductors joke that he is thorough. He does not correct them.

He carries a small card in his wallet with the date of the incident written on it. He does not know why. He will never show it to anyone. But sometimes, alone in the cab between stations, he takes it out and looks at the numbers, and for a moment he is back in that Tuesday afternoon, the brake lever cold in his palm, the world stopped still.
